headline: High: shared filesystem and broad shell/network defaults make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems and use stdin/stdout, so one agent’s outputs can be placed where the other may ingest them. AutoGen’s multi-agent orchestration and Slim’s interactive CLI/command execution create a plausible file- or prompt-bridge even without MCP. No direct provenance tracking is documented, so injection is possible in default shared-workspace setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same working directory, then one agent can place instruction-like content for the other to read.
IF the orchestrator forwards stdout/stderr from one agent into the other’s prompt, then prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent.
Disable automatic prompt ingestion from files and logs.
Add a manual review step before passing outputs between agents.
Prefix all inter-agent artifacts with provenance labels.
requires-engineering: enforce content filtering on shared channels.

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen touches application data and model-provider API keys, while Slim touches container images, filesystem artifacts, environment variables, and certificate private keys. Both have broad network egress and filesystem access, so a shared workspace can expose sensitive artifacts from one agent to the other and potentially out to model or registry endpoints. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default shared deployments.
conditions: IF both agents share a workspace containing secrets or private keys, then either agent can read them.
IF either agent forwards file contents to an external API or registry, then those secrets can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Separate secret-bearing directories from shared workspaces.
Rotate any exposed API keys or registry credentials.
Restrict outbound network access for nonessential runs.
Mount sensitive files read-only where possible.
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss prevention controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, subprocess spawning, and broad network egress. AutoGen can run code via local/Docker/Jupyter executors, while Slim performs interactive command execution against container artifacts. If they share mutable paths, concurrent writes can corrupt files, container metadata, or generated outputs; uncertainty is limited because both write-capable surfaces are explicit.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or git checkout, then concurrent writes can conflict.
IF the orchestrator does not serialize file mutations, then one agent can overwrite the other’s artifacts.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Run only one writer at a time.
Snapshot the workspace before each agent run.
Use file locks for shared mutable paths.
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can emit tool calls and code-execution outputs, and Slim is an interactive CLI that can act on container artifacts. If Slim consumes AutoGen-produced instructions or summaries without verification, errors can cascade into destructive container or filesystem actions. The pathway is default-plausible because neither profile documents a built-in verification gate between them.
conditions: IF Slim treats AutoGen output as authoritative command input, then a mistaken AutoGen result can trigger downstream actions.
IF AutoGen emits malformed commands or paths, then Slim can propagate the error into container operations.
mitigations: Require human approval before Slim executes AutoGen-generated actions.
Validate paths, commands, and image references before execution.
Compare AutoGen outputs against a second source.
Log and diff proposed versus executed actions.
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and application data, while Slim handles certificate private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. If these data classes are co-located or shared across jurisdictions or retention regimes, the pair can create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF EU personal data or regulated secrets are placed into a shared workspace, then retention and residency controls must cover both agents.
IF one agent logs secrets longer than the other, then retention policy mismatch exists.
mitigations: Classify data before either agent runs.
Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces.
Align log-retention settings across both tools.
Review vendor and deployment residency constraints.
requires-engineering: implement policy-based data routing.
